migration-django-upgrade.title: How to upgrade Django to a newer version
migration-django-upgrade.source:
========================================
How to upgrade Django to a newer version
========================================

Upgrading Django to the latest version offers several benefits:

* New features and improvements become available.
* Bugs are fixed.
* Older versions of Django eventually stop receiving security updates
  (see :ref:`supported-versions-policy`).
* Upgrading with each new release helps keep your code base current and makes
  future upgrades smoother.

.. admonition:: Tools to help with version upgrades

    Django has a vibrant ecosystem. There are automated upgrade helpers
    highlighted on the `Community Ecosystem
    <https://www.djangoproject.com/community/ecosystem/#upgrade-utilities>`__
    page.

Here are some things to consider to help make your upgrade process as smooth as
possible.

Required Reading
================

If it's your first time doing an upgrade, it is useful to read the :doc:`guide
on the different release processes </internals/release-process>`.

Afterward, you should familiarize yourself with the changes that were made in
the new Django version(s):

* Read the :doc:`release notes </releases/index>` for each 'final' release from
  the one after your current Django version, up to and including the version to
  which you plan to upgrade.
* Look at the :doc:`deprecation timeline</internals/deprecation>` for the
  relevant versions.

Pay particular attention to backwards incompatible changes to get a clear idea
of what will be needed for a successful upgrade.

If you're upgrading through more than one feature version (e.g. 2.0 to 2.2),
it's usually easier to upgrade through each feature release incrementally
(2.0 to 2.1 to 2.2) rather than to make all the changes for each feature
release at once. For each feature release, use the latest patch release (e.g.
for 2.1, use 2.1.15).

The same incremental upgrade approach is recommended when upgrading from one
LTS to the next.

Dependencies
============

In most cases it will be necessary to upgrade to the latest version of your
Django-related dependencies as well. If the Django version was recently
released or if some of your dependencies are not well-maintained, some of your
dependencies may not yet support the new Django version. In these cases you may
have to wait until new versions of your dependencies are released.

Resolving deprecation warnings
==============================

Before upgrading, it's a good idea to resolve any deprecation warnings raised
by your project while using your current version of Django. Fixing these
warnings before upgrading ensures that you're informed about areas of the code
that need altering.

In Python, deprecation warnings are silenced by default. You must turn them on
using the ``-Wa`` Python command line option or the :envvar:`PYTHONWARNINGS`
environment variable. For example, to show warnings while running tests:

.. console::

    $ python -Wa manage.py test

If you're not using the Django test runner, you may need to also ensure that
any console output is not captured which would hide deprecation warnings. For
example, if you use `pytest <https://docs.pytest.org/>`__:

.. code-block:: console

    $ PYTHONWARNINGS=always pytest tests --capture=no

Resolve any deprecation warnings with your current version of Django before
continuing the upgrade process.

Third party applications might use deprecated APIs in order to support multiple
versions of Django, so deprecation warnings in packages you've installed don't
necessarily indicate a problem. If a package doesn't support the latest version
of Django, consider raising an issue or sending a pull request for it.

Installation
============

Once you're ready, it is time to :doc:`install the new Django version
</topics/install>`. If you are using a :mod:`virtual environment <venv>` and it
is a major upgrade, you might want to set up a new environment with all the
dependencies first.

If you installed Django with pip_, you can use the ``--upgrade`` or ``-U``
flag:

.. console::

   $ python -m pip install -U Django

.. _pip: https://pip.pypa.io/

Testing
=======

When the new environment is set up, :doc:`run the full test suite
</topics/testing/overview>` for your application. Again, it's useful to turn
on deprecation warnings on so they're shown in the test output (you can also
use the flag if you test your app manually using ``manage.py runserver``):

.. console::

    $ python -Wa manage.py test

After you have run the tests, fix any failures. While you have the release
notes fresh in your mind, it may also be a good time to take advantage of new
features in Django by refactoring your code to eliminate any deprecation
warnings.

If you are upgrading to an alpha, beta, or release candidate, please see our
guide on :ref:`testing-pre-releases` for more specific tips about catching
regressions and reporting bugs.

Deployment
==========

When you are sufficiently confident your app works with the new version of
Django, you're ready to go ahead and :doc:`deploy </howto/deployment/index>`
your upgraded Django project.

If you are using caching provided by Django, you should consider clearing your
cache after upgrading. Otherwise you may run into problems, for example, if you
are caching pickled objects as these objects are not guaranteed to be
pickle-compatible across Django versions. A past instance of incompatibility
was caching pickled :class:`~django.http.HttpResponse` objects, either directly
or indirectly via the :func:`~django.views.decorators.cache.cache_page`
decorator.

use the latest patch release. For 2.1, use 2.1.15.

Use the same step-by-step method when you upgrade from one LTS to the next.

Dependencies
============

In most cases you must also upgrade your Django-related dependencies to their
latest version. Some dependencies may not yet support the new Django version.
This happens when Django released the version recently, or when a maintainer
does not keep the dependency current. In these cases you must wait for the new
versions of your dependencies.

Resolving deprecation warnings
==============================

Before you upgrade, resolve the deprecation warnings that your project raises
on your current version of Django. Fixing them first shows you which parts of
the code you must change.

Python hides deprecation warnings by default. Turn them on with the ``-Wa``
Python command line option or the :envvar:`PYTHONWARNINGS` environment
variable. For example, to show warnings while you run tests:

.. console::

    $ python -Wa manage.py test

If you do not use the Django test runner, also make sure that nothing captures
the console output, because that hides the deprecation warnings. For example,
with `pytest <https://docs.pytest.org/>`__:

.. code-block:: console

    $ PYTHONWARNINGS=always pytest tests --capture=no

Resolve every deprecation warning on your current version of Django before you
continue.

A third party application may use deprecated APIs to support several versions
of Django. A deprecation warning in a package you installed does not always
mean a problem. If a package does not support the latest version of Django,
consider that you raise an issue or send a pull request for it.

Installation
============

Now :doc:`install the new Django version </topics/install>`. If you use a
:mod:`virtual environment <venv>` and this is a major upgrade, you may want to
set up a new environment with all the dependencies first.

If you installed Django with pip_, use the ``--upgrade`` or ``-U`` flag:

.. console::

   $ python -m pip install -U Django

.. _pip: https://pip.pypa.io/

Testing
=======

After you set up the new environment, :doc:`run the full test suite
</topics/testing/overview>` for your application. Turn on deprecation warnings
again so the test output shows them. You can also use the flag when you test
your app by hand with ``manage.py runserver``:

.. console::

    $ python -Wa manage.py test

Fix every failure after you run the tests. The release notes are fresh in your
mind, so this is also a good time to use the new features in Django. Refactor
your code to remove any deprecation warnings.

If you upgrade to an alpha, beta, or release candidate, see our guide on
:ref:`testing-pre-releases`. It gives more tips about how you catch regressions
and report bugs.

Deployment
==========

When you are confident that your app works with the new version of Django,
:doc:`deploy </howto/deployment/index>` your upgraded Django project.

If you use the caching that Django gives, consider that you clear your cache
after the upgrade. If you do not, you may hit problems. For example, pickled
objects in the cache are not guaranteed to stay pickle-compatible across Django
versions. One past example of this incompatibility was the cache of pickled
:class:`~django.http.HttpResponse` objects, either directly or through the
:func:`~django.views.decorators.cache.cache_page` decorator.

========================================
How to upgrade Django to a newer version
========================================

An upgrade to the latest version of Django gives you these benefits:

* You get new features and improvements.
* You get fixes for bugs.
* Old versions of Django stop receiving security updates in the end
  (see :ref:`supported-versions-policy`).

  makes each future upgrade easier.

postmortem-chia-mempool-fastforward.source:
# Block creation impacted due to mempool issues.

## Issue Summary

Farmers that are eligible to create the next block have a limited time (approximately 28 seconds) to create an unfinished block and via network propagation get this to a timelord that will infuse the unfinished block to construct the finished block.

Farmers will take transactions from the mempool ordered by fee per cost, and add them into the unfinished block as a way to benefit from fees attached to transactions that go to the farmer making the block.

CNI detected that while the mempool was completely full, transactions were not being included in blocks. Additionally, block production slowed down versus expected production rate. It was determined that farmers eligible to create blocks were not creating unfinished blocks in time due to several bugs in the mempool logic around fast forward spends.

Fast forward spends are a way for a singleton transaction to be able to apply to future versions of the singleton.

Fast forward spends enable offer files to refer to singletons by coin ID, even though the coin ID changes for every state update.

In addition, fast forward spends are used for vaults. Because the vault singleton is used to authorize all coins belonging to it, it would be too limiting to only be able to have one vault spend “in-flight” at a time. Fast forward allows multiple spends of the vault singleton to be in the mempool concurrently, and farmers deduplicate and rebase them sequentially as they create blocks.


CNI determined the following issues were the root cause of the block creation slow down:
* 1. Fast forward spends don’t become invalid just because their coin is spent. They can be fast-forwarded to the latest version of the singleton. Fast-forward spends rely on other parts of the spend bundle for being evicted  (e.g. that coin is spent by a block). We failed to consider the case where the only spend in a bundle was a fast-forward spend, it would not be evicted after the singleton was melted. 
* 2. FF-Spends enter the mempool even if their coin is already spent. When we form the block they will be fast-forwarded on top of the latest version of the singleton. However, we failed to validate that the singleton still existed. I.e. we would accept singleton spends into the mempool for singletons which have been melted and no longer exist.
* 3. When we formed a block, FF spends would be updated to spend the most recent coin of a singleton. This update was done in place, causing the mempool to change and propagate the fast-forwarded versions of the mempool item to the rest of the network. This would cause the mempool item to duplicate (double in numbers) every time a farmer tried to form a block.

With these 3 bugs, someone submitting a singleton spend that’s eligible for fast forward, without bundling it with any other spend would:
* Be considered valid and enter the mempool and propagate throughout the network.
* Whenever a farmer would make a block, it would multiply the spend, propagating the new transactions throughout the network (3)
* Trying to stop the spread by melting the singleton makes the transactions not go through, but the spends were not evicted from the mempool (2). In our scenario, mempool was full of these spends when this happened. All of these spends failed during block creation, causing farmers to time-out before finding any valid transactions.
* Farmers trying to create a block with the affected mempool items would experience performance issues leading them to miss the cutoff time for their block to be included in the blockchain.

02-13-2025 11:00 pm - Mempool spendbundle count started slowly increasing.

02-14-2025 11:30 am - Mempool cost hits max cost.

02-14-2025 1:10 pm - Mempool spendbundle count plateaus at ~6200.

02-14-2025 4:45 pm - The Chia blockchain netspace started decreasing and timelord infused blocks per minute had a marked drop.

02-14-2025 11:00 pm - The cause of the issues were diagnosed by CNI and a hotfix release of the chia blockchain software was prepared.

02-15-2025 1:30 am - The hotfix release of the Chia blockchain software build process was initiated.

02-15-2025 3:00 am - The hotfix release of the Chia blockchain software deployment completed as version 2.5.1

02-19-2025 3:15 pm - Version 2.5.2 was released that included the bug fixes for the Fast Forward issues detailed in the Issue Summary.

# Mempool Bugs Slowed Block Creation

## Issue Summary

A farmer eligible to create the next block has about 28 seconds to build an unfinished block and propagate it across the network to a timelord, who infuses it to produce the finished block.

Farmers pull transactions from the mempool, ordered by fee per cost, and add them to the unfinished block — this is how the farmer earns the fees attached to those transactions.

CNI observed that the mempool was completely full, yet transactions were not making it into blocks. Block production also slowed below the expected rate. The cause: several bugs in the mempool's fast forward spend logic were preventing eligible farmers from building unfinished blocks in time.

A fast forward spend lets a singleton transaction apply to future versions of that singleton.

This is what allows offer files to refer to singletons by coin ID, even though the coin ID changes with every state update.

Fast forward spends are also used by vaults. The vault singleton authorizes every coin belonging to it, so allowing only one vault spend "in-flight" at a time would be too limiting. Fast forward lets multiple spends of the vault singleton sit in the mempool at once; farmers deduplicate and rebase them sequentially as they build blocks.

CNI identified three root causes of the slowdown:

* 1. **A spent coin does not invalidate a fast forward spend.** Such a spend can simply be fast-forwarded to the latest version of the singleton, so eviction depends on other parts of the spend bundle (for example, that coin being spent by a block). We did not consider the case where a bundle's only spend was a fast-forward spend — it would never be evicted after the singleton was melted.
* 2. **FF-spends enter the mempool even when their coin is already spent.** At block formation they get fast-forwarded onto the latest version of the singleton, but we never validated that the singleton still existed. So we accepted singleton spends for singletons that had been melted and no longer existed.
* 3. **Rebasing during block formation mutated the mempool.** FF spends were updated in place to spend the singleton's most recent coin, which changed the mempool and propagated the fast-forwarded versions of the item to the rest of the network. The mempool item therefore doubled in number every time a farmer tried to form a block.

Together, these three bugs meant that anyone submitting a fast-forward-eligible singleton spend, unbundled with any other spend, would see the following:

* The spend was considered valid, entered the mempool, and propagated across the network.
* Every time a farmer made a block, the spend multiplied, propagating the new transactions across the network (bug 3).
* Melting the singleton to stop the spread stopped the transactions from going through, but did not evict the spends from the mempool (bug 2). * Farmers building a block from the affected mempool items hit performance problems and missed the cutoff time for their block to be included in the blockchain.

**02-14-2025 11:30 am** — Mempool cost hit max cost.

**02-14-2025 1:10 pm** — Mempool spendbundle count plateaued at ~6200.

**02-14-2025 4:45 pm** — Chia blockchain netspace began decreasing; timelord infused blocks per minute dropped markedly.

**02-15-2025 1:30 am** — Hotfix release build process started.

| 02-15-2025 1:30 am | The build process for the hotfix release started. |
| 02-15-2025 3:00 am | The deployment of the hotfix release finished as version 2.5.1. |

## Resolution and recovery

The Chia blockchain is decentralized, and many nodes run different configurations and versions. The fast forward bugs therefore did not affect most of the blockchain netspace.

Version 2.5.1 contains a workaround that caps the time to create an unfinished block. The cap makes sure the unfinished block reaches a timelord in time. The blockchain netspace started to recover towards previous levels after the release of v2.5.1.

Version 2.5.2 included three fixes. These fixes made the mempool items from the fast forward bugs invalid. The mempool cleared these items as the user base took up v2.5.2.

1. The mempool rejects a spend bundle that contains only fast forward spends.
2. When a spend is rebased on top of the latest version of the singleton, we do not update the item in the mempool. This removes the risk of distributing the new copy to the network.
3. When the mempool ingests a spend bundle, it checks every spend that is eligible for fast forward. The check makes sure the latest version of the singleton still exists, with the given puzzle hash.

# Block creation slowed by mempool problems

## Issue summary

A farmer that is eligible to create the next block has about 28 seconds to do two things. The farmer must create an unfinished block. The network must then propagate that block to a timelord, which infuses it to make the finished block.

A farmer takes transactions from the mempool in order of fee per cost. The farmer adds them to the unfinished block. The fees attached to those transactions go to the farmer that makes the block.

CNI found that the mempool was completely full, but blocks did not include the transactions. Block production also slowed below the expected rate. Farmers that were eligible to create blocks did not create unfinished blocks in time. Several bugs in the mempool logic for fast forward spends caused this.

A fast forward spend lets a singleton transaction apply to future versions of the singleton. Fast forward spends let offer files refer to singletons by coin ID, even though the coin ID changes at every state update.

Vaults also use fast forward spends. The vault singleton authorizes all coins that belong to it. One vault spend "in-flight" at a time is too limiting. Fast forward lets several spends of the vault singleton sit in the mempool at the same time. Farmers deduplicate these spends and rebase them in order as they create blocks.

CNI found these three root causes of the slow block creation:

1. A fast forward spend does not become invalid when its coin is spent. The spend can move forward to the latest version of the singleton. A fast forward spend relies on other parts of the spend bundle for eviction. For example, a block spends that coin. We did not consider the case where a fast forward spend was the only spend in a bundle. That bundle was not evicted after someone melted the singleton.
2. A fast forward spend enters the mempool even if its coin is already spent. When we form the block, the spend moves forward onto the latest version of the singleton. We did not check that the singleton still existed. We accepted singleton spends into the mempool for singletons that were melted and no longer exist.
3. When we formed a block, a fast forward spend was updated to spend the most recent coin of a singleton. This update happened in place. The mempool changed, and it propagated the fast-forwarded versions of the mempool item to the rest of the network. The mempool item doubled in number every time a farmer tried to form a block.

- The spend is valid. It enters the mempool and propagates through the network.
- Every time a farmer makes a block, the spend multiplies. The new transactions propagate through the network. This is bug 3.
- Melting the singleton stops the transactions from going through, but it does not evict the spends from the mempool. This is bug 2. In our case, the mempool was full of these spends when this happened. All of these spends failed during block creation. Farmers timed out before they found any valid transaction.
- A farmer that tried to create a block with the affected mempool items hit performance problems. The farmer missed the cutoff time for the block to enter the blockchain.

postmortem-chia-clvm-cost.title: Unbound CLVM cost restriction on mempool
postmortem-chia-clvm-cost.source:
# unbound CLVM cost restriction on mempool

## Issue Summary

Transactions that are included in a block are aggregated from one or more spendbundles. Inside spendbundles coins are spent, with the reveal of the puzzle and their solution of the coins. The puzzles and solutions consist of CLVM code that is assigned a cost, based on bytes of the code, and usage of operands and conditions. Each node on the network runs the CLVM code with limitations on how much resources the execution can use up via restrictions on the CLVM cost.

The Chia default mempool code uses a CLVM cost restriction of 0.5 times the restriction that consensus uses (what is allowed in a block). The consensus constant is "MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM": 11000000000


Version 1.7.1 of the mempool doesn’t include verification code that the CLVM cost of a MempoolItem has to be <= `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`
This code was present in previous versions.

This verification code was removed because it was assumed that running the MempoolItem as a block generator would perform this check already, making the code redundant.

The chia_rs function called run_block_generator() contained a bug where if the byte cost exceeded the limit (5.5 billion in this case), the u64 wraps around and effectively removes the cost limit.

The removal of the verification in the mempool code and the chia_rs bug combined allowed for a MempoolItem to have an unbound CLVM cost when the byte cost exceeded the limit.

## Timeline (all times PST)   04/23/2023 - 05/03/2023. All times approximations

04/23/2023 - Mempool items with a cost exceeding `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5` were reported by a community member in keybase.

05/03/2023 - Version 1.8.0 of the Chia blockchain was released with fixes for the mempool code and chia_rs.


## Resolution and recovery

This issue was addressed in 1.8.0 by: 

Reinstating the mempool verification code that the CLVM cost of a MempoolItem has to be <= `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`.

Fixing the cost calculation in chia_rs when the byte cost exceeds the limit.


The issue was present in mainnet and manifested itself by transactions being added to the mempool that exceeded the CLVM cost threshold. These transactions were not added to blocks as consensus checks on CLVM cost disallowed that.

Chia monitored the mempool for these excessive CLVM cost mempool items and found that they were limited in scope and barely exceeded the threshold limit, causing very limited impact on nodes on the network during the time that the mempool allowed them.

# Unbounded CLVM Cost Restriction on the Mempool

## Issue Summary

Blocks contain transactions aggregated from one or more spendbundles. Inside a spendbundle, coins are spent by revealing the coin's puzzle and its solution. Puzzles and solutions are CLVM code, and each is assigned a cost based on the size of the code in bytes and its use of operands and conditions. Every node on the network runs this CLVM code under limits on how many resources the execution may consume, enforced as restrictions on the CLVM cost.

The Chia default mempool code uses a CLVM cost restriction of 0.5 times the restriction that consensus uses (what is allowed in a block). The consensus constant is `"MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM": 11000000000`.

Three things combined to cause the issue:

1. **Missing mempool check.** Version 1.7.1 of the mempool does not include the verification code requiring a MempoolItem's CLVM cost to be `<= constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`. This code was present in previous versions. It was removed on the assumption that running the MempoolItem as a block generator would already perform the check, making it redundant.
2. **chia_rs bug.** The chia_rs function `run_block_generator()` contained a bug: when the byte cost exceeded the limit (5.5 billion in this case), the u64 wrapped around, effectively removing the cost limit.
3. **Result.** Together, the removed mempool verification and the chia_rs bug allowed a MempoolItem to have an unbounded CLVM cost whenever the byte cost exceeded the limit.

## Timeline

All times PST and approximate. 04/23/2023 – 05/03/2023.

- **04/23/2023** — A community member reported, on keybase, mempool items with a cost exceeding `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`.
- **05/03/2023** — Version 1.8.0 of the Chia blockchain was released with fixes for the mempool code and chia_rs.

## Resolution and Recovery

Version 1.8.0 addressed the issue by:

- Reinstating the mempool verification code requiring a MempoolItem's CLVM cost to be `<= constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`.
- Fixing the cost calculation in chia_rs for when the byte cost exceeds the limit.

The issue was present on mainnet. It showed up as transactions being added to the mempool that exceeded the CLVM cost threshold. Those transactions were never added to blocks, because consensus checks on CLVM cost disallowed it.

Chia monitored the mempool for these excessive-cost items and found they were limited in scope and barely exceeded the threshold limit. Impact on nodes on the network was very limited during the time the mempool allowed them.

Version 1.7.1 of the mempool let a MempoolItem hold an unbound CLVM cost. Two faults combined to cause this. The mempool lost a check, and `chia_rs` had a bug.

A block aggregates one or more spendbundles. A spendbundle spends coins. Each spend reveals the puzzle of the coin and the solution of the coin. Puzzles and solutions consist of CLVM code.

Each piece of CLVM code carries a cost. The cost comes from the bytes of the code, the operands, and the conditions. Every node on the network runs the CLVM code. The CLVM cost restriction limits the resources that the execution can use.

The default mempool code of Chia uses a CLVM cost restriction of 0.5 times the restriction of consensus. The consensus restriction is what a block allows. The consensus constant is `"MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM": 11000000000`.

Version 1.7.1 of the mempool does not include the code that checks that the CLVM cost of a MempoolItem is <= `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`. Earlier versions included this code. A developer removed it because running the MempoolItem as a block generator was assumed to make this check already, so the code looked redundant.

The `chia_rs` function `run_block_generator()` contained a bug. When the byte cost exceeded the limit of 5.5 billion, the u64 wrapped around. The wrap effectively removed the cost limit.

All times are PST, from 04/23/2023 to 05/03/2023. All times are approximations.

Version 1.8.0 addressed the issue in two ways:

1. It reinstated the mempool code that checks that the CLVM cost of a MempoolItem is <= `constants.MAX_BLOCK_COST_CLVM * 0.5`.
2. It fixed the cost calculation in `chia_rs` for the case where the byte cost exceeds the limit.

runbook-etcd-restore.title: Restoring, upgrading, and maintaining an etcd cluster
runbook-etcd-restore.source:
## Restoring an etcd cluster

If any API servers are running in your cluster, you should not attempt to
restore instances of etcd. Instead, follow these steps to restore etcd:

- stop *all* API server instances
- restore state in all etcd instances
- restart all API server instances

The Kubernetes project also recommends restarting Kubernetes components (`kube-scheduler`,
`kube-controller-manager`, `kubelet`) to ensure that they don't rely on some
stale data. In practice the restore takes a bit of time.  During the
restoration, critical components will lose leader lock and restart themselves.

etcd supports restoring from snapshots that are taken from an etcd process of
the [major.minor](https://semver.org/) version. Restoring a version from a
different patch version of etcd is also supported. A restore operation is
employed to recover the data of a failed cluster.

Before starting the restore operation, a snapshot file must be present. It can
either be a snapshot file from a previous backup operation, or from a remaining
[data directory](https://etcd.io/docs/current/op-guide/configuration/#--data-dir).

   When restoring the cluster using [`etcdutl`](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/main/etcdutl/README.md),
   use the `--data-dir` option to specify to which folder the cluster should be restored:

   ```shell
   etcdutl --data-dir <data-dir-location> snapshot restore snapshot.db
   ```
   where `<data-dir-location>` is a directory that will be created during the restore process.


   The usage of `etcdctl` for restoring has been **deprecated** since etcd v3.5.x and is slated for removal from etcd v3.6.
   It is recommended to utilize [`etcdutl`](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/main/etcdutl/README.md) instead.

   The below example depicts the usage of the `etcdctl` tool for the restore operation:

   ```shell
   export ETCDCTL_API=3
   etcdctl --data-dir <data-dir-location> snapshot restore snapshot.db
   ```

   If `<data-dir-location>` is the same folder as before, delete it and stop the etcd process before restoring the cluster. 
   Otherwise, change etcd configuration and restart the etcd process after restoration to have it use the new data directory:
   first change  `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml`'s `volumes.hostPath.path` for `name: etcd-data`  to `<data-dir-location>`,
   then execute `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod <name-of-etcd-pod>` or `systemctl restart kubelet.service` (or both).


For more information and examples on restoring a cluster from a snapshot file, see
[etcd disaster recovery documentation](https://etcd.io/docs/current/op-guide/recovery/#restoring-a-cluster).

If the access URLs of the restored cluster are changed from the previous
cluster, the Kubernetes API server must be reconfigured accordingly. In this
case, restart Kubernetes API servers with the flag
`--etcd-servers=$NEW_ETCD_CLUSTER` instead of the flag
`--etcd-servers=$OLD_ETCD_CLUSTER`. Replace `$NEW_ETCD_CLUSTER` and
`$OLD_ETCD_CLUSTER` with the respective IP addresses. If a load balancer is
used in front of an etcd cluster, you might need to update the load balancer
instead.

If the majority of etcd members have permanently failed, the etcd cluster is
considered failed. In this scenario, Kubernetes cannot make any changes to its
current state. Although the scheduled pods might continue to run, no new pods
can be scheduled. In such cases, recover the etcd cluster and potentially
reconfigure Kubernetes API servers to fix the issue.


## Upgrading etcd clusters

Before you start an upgrade, back up your etcd cluster first.

For details on etcd upgrade, refer to the [etcd upgrades](https://etcd.io/docs/latest/upgrades/) documentation.

## Maintaining etcd clusters

For more details on etcd maintenance, please refer to the [etcd maintenance](https://etcd.io/docs/latest/op-guide/maintenance/) documentation.

runbook-cassandra-repair.title: Repair
runbook-cassandra-repair.source:
== Incremental and Full Repairs

There are 2 types of repairs: full repairs, and incremental repairs.
Full repairs operate over all of the data in the token range being
repaired. Incremental repairs only repair data that's been written since
the previous incremental repair.

Incremental repairs are the default repair type, and if run regularly,
can significantly reduce the time and io cost of performing a repair.
However, it's important to understand that once an incremental repair
marks data as repaired, it won't try to repair it again. This is fine
for syncing up missed writes, but it doesn't protect against things like
disk corruption, data loss by operator error, or bugs in Cassandra. For
this reason, full repairs should still be run occasionally.

== Automated Repair Scheduling

Since repair can result in a lot of disk and network io, it has
traditionally not been run automatically by Cassandra.

In the latest version of Cassandra, a new feature called
xref:managing/operating/auto_repair.adoc[auto repair] was introduced to
allow Cassandra to submit and manage repairs automatically on a schedule.

The introduction of this feature does not interfere with existing repair
functionality enabled via nodetool.

== Submitting Repairs Using Nodetool

Repairs can also be run by the operator via nodetool.

Incremental repair is the default and is run with the following command:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair
----

A full repair can be run with the following command:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair --full
----

Additionally, repair can be run on a single keyspace:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair [options] <keyspace_name>
----

Or even on specific tables:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair [options] <keyspace_name> <table1> <table2>
----


The repair command repairs token ranges only on the node being repaired; it does not repair the whole cluster.
By default, repair operates on all token ranges replicated by the node on which repair is run, causing duplicate work when running it on every node. Avoid duplicate work by using the `-pr` flag to repair only the "primary" ranges on a node. 
Do a full cluster repair by running the `nodetool repair -pr` command on each node in each datacenter in the cluster, until all of the nodes and datacenters are repaired. 

The specific frequency of repair that's right for your cluster, of
course, depends on several factors. However, if you're just starting out
and looking for somewhere to start, running an incremental repair every
1-3 days, and a full repair every 1-3 weeks is probably reasonable. If
you don't want to run incremental repairs, a full repair every 5 days is
a good place to start.

At a minimum, repair should be run often enough that the gc grace period
never expires on unrepaired data. Otherwise, deleted data could
reappear. With a default gc grace period of 10 days, repairing every
node in your cluster at least once every 7 days will prevent this, while
providing enough slack to allow for delays.

== Other Options

`-pr, --partitioner-range`::
  Restricts repair to the 'primary' token ranges of the node being
  repaired. A primary range is just a token range for which a node is
  the first replica in the ring.
`-prv, --preview`::
  Estimates the amount of streaming that would occur for the given
  repair command. This builds the merkle trees, and prints the expected
  streaming activity, but does not actually do any streaming. By
  default, incremental repairs are estimated, add the `--full` flag to
  estimate a full repair.
`-vd, --validate`::
  Verifies that the repaired data is the same across all nodes. Similar
  to `--preview`, this builds and compares merkle trees of repaired
  data, but doesn't do any streaming. This is useful for
  troubleshooting. If this shows that the repaired data is out of sync,
  a full repair should be run.

`nodetool repair docs <nodetool_repair>`

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair
----

Run a full repair with this command:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair --full
----

You can also run repair on a single keyspace:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair [options] <keyspace_name>
----

You can run repair on specific tables:

[source,none]
----
nodetool repair [options] <keyspace_name> <table1> <table2>
----

The repair command repairs token ranges on the node that you repair. It does not repair the whole cluster.

By default, repair covers all token ranges that the node replicates. This causes duplicate work when you run it on every node. Use the `-pr` flag to repair only the "primary" ranges on a node, and you avoid the duplicate work.

To repair the full cluster, run the `nodetool repair -pr` command on each node in each datacenter. Continue until you repair all the nodes and all the datacenters.

The right frequency of repair for your cluster depends on several factors. If you start out and need a first choice, an incremental repair every 1-3 days and a full repair every 1-3 weeks is likely reasonable. If you do not want to run incremental repairs, a full repair every 5 days is a good first choice.

At a minimum, run repair often enough that the gc grace period never expires on unrepaired data. If it expires, deleted data can reappear. The default gc grace period is 10 days. Repair every node in your cluster at least once every 7 days to prevent this. The 7 day period gives you enough slack for delays.

== Other Options

`-pr, --partitioner-range`::
  Limits repair to the 'primary' token ranges of the node that you repair. A primary range is a token range for which a node is the first replica in the ring.

`-vd, --validate`::
  Checks that the repaired data is the same across all nodes. Like `--preview`, this builds and compares merkle trees of repaired data, but does no streaming. This helps you troubleshoot. If it shows that the repaired data is out of sync, run a full repair.

A repair can cause a lot of disk io and network io. For this reason, Cassandra has traditionally not run repairs automatically.

The latest version of Cassandra adds a new feature called

This feature does not interfere with the existing repair functionality that you start with nodetool.

howto-k8s-debug-pods.title: Debug Pods
howto-k8s-debug-pods.source:
### Debugging Pods

The first step in debugging a Pod is taking a look at it. Check the current
state of the Pod and recent events with the following command:

```shell
kubectl describe pods ${POD_NAME}
```

Look at the state of the containers in the pod. Are they all `Running`?
Have there been recent restarts?

Continue debugging depending on the state of the pods.

#### My pod stays pending

If a Pod is stuck in `Pending` it means that it can not be scheduled onto a node.
Generally this is because there are insufficient resources of one type or another
that prevent scheduling. Look at the output of the `kubectl describe ...` command above.
There should be messages from the scheduler about why it can not schedule your pod.
Reasons include:

* **You don't have enough resources**: You may have exhausted the supply of CPU
  or Memory in your cluster, in this case you need to delete Pods, adjust resource
  requests, or add new nodes to your cluster. See [Compute Resources document](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/)
  for more information.

* **You are using `hostPort`**: When you bind a Pod to a `hostPort` there are a
  limited number of places that pod can be scheduled. In most cases, `hostPort`
  is unnecessary, try using a Service object to expose your Pod.  If you do require
  `hostPort` then you can only schedule as many Pods as there are nodes in your Kubernetes cluster.


#### My pod stays waiting

If a Pod is stuck in the `Waiting` state, then it has been scheduled to a worker node, 
but it can't run on that machine. Again, the information from `kubectl describe ...`
should be informative. The most common cause of `Waiting` pods is a failure to pull the image.
There are three things to check:

* Make sure that you have the name of the image correct.
* Have you pushed the image to the registry?
* Try to manually pull the image to see if the image can be pulled. For example,
  if you use Docker on your PC, run `docker pull <image>`.


#### My pod stays terminating

If a Pod is stuck in the `Terminating` state, it means that a deletion has been
issued for the Pod, but the control plane is unable to delete the Pod object.

This typically happens if the Pod has a [finalizer](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/finalizers/)
and there is an [admission webhook](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/)
installed in the cluster that prevents the control plane from removing the
finalizer.

To identify this scenario, check if your cluster has any
ValidatingWebhookConfiguration or MutatingWebhookConfiguration that target
`UPDATE` operations for `pods` resources.

If the webhook is provided by a third-party:
- Make sure you are using the latest version.
- Disable the webhook for `UPDATE` operations.
- Report an issue with the corresponding provider.

If you are the author of the webhook:
- For a mutating webhook, make sure it never changes immutable fields on
  `UPDATE` operations. For example, changes to containers are usually not allowed.
- For a validating webhook, make sure that your validation policies only apply
  to new changes. In other words, you should allow Pods with existing violations
  to pass validation. This allows Pods that were created before the validating
  webhook was installed to continue running.

#### My pod is crashing or otherwise unhealthy

Once your pod has been scheduled, the methods described in
[Debug Running Pods](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod/)
are available for debugging.

#### My pod is running but not doing what I told it to do

If your pod is not behaving as you expected, it may be that there was an error in your
pod description (e.g. `mypod.yaml` file on your local machine), and that the error
was silently ignored when you created the pod.  Often a section of the pod description
is nested incorrectly, or a key name is typed incorrectly, and so the key is ignored.
For example, if you misspelled `command` as `commnd` then the pod will be created but
will not use the command line you intended it to use.

The first thing to do is to delete your pod and try creating it again with the `--validate` option.
For example, run `kubectl apply --validate -f mypod.yaml`.
If you misspelled `command` as `commnd` then will give an error like this:

```shell
I0805 10:43:25.129850   46757 schema.go:126] unknown field: commnd
I0805 10:43:25.129973   46757 schema.go:129] this may be a false alarm, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/6842
pods/mypod
```

<!-- TODO: Now that #11914 is merged, this advice may need to be updated -->

The next thing to check is whether the pod on the apiserver
matches the pod you meant to create (e.g. in a yaml file on your local machine).
For example, run `kubectl get pods/mypod -o yaml > mypod-on-apiserver.yaml` and then
manually compare the original pod description, `mypod.yaml` with the one you got
back from apiserver, `mypod-on-apiserver.yaml`. There will typically be some
lines on the "apiserver" version that are not on the original version. This is
expected. However, if there are lines on the original that are not on the apiserver
version, then this may indicate a problem with your pod spec.

Then continue to debug based on the state of the Pod.

* **You do not have enough resources**: The cluster may have no CPU or memory left. In this case you must delete Pods, change the requests for resources, or add new nodes to the cluster. See the [Compute Resources document](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/) for more information.

A Pod that stays in `Waiting` is scheduled to a worker node, but it cannot run on that machine. Again, the output of `kubectl describe ...` tells you more. The most common cause is a failure to pull the image.

2. Check that you pushed the image to the registry.
3. Pull the image by hand to see whether the pull works. For example, if you use Docker on your PC, run `docker pull <image>`.

pods/mypod

troubleshoot-etcd-failures.title: etcd failure modes
troubleshoot-etcd-failures.source:
---
title: Failure modes
weight: 4250
description: Kinds of failures and etcd's tolerance for them
---

Failures are common in a large deployment of machines. A machine fails when its hardware or software malfunctions. Multiple machines fail together when there are power failures or network issues. Multiple kinds of failures can also happen at once; it is almost impossible to enumerate all possible failure cases.

In this section, we catalog kinds of failures and discuss how etcd is designed to tolerate these failures. Most users, if not all, can map a particular failure into one kind of failure. To prepare for rare or [unrecoverable failures][unrecoverable], always [back up][backup] the etcd cluster.

## Minor followers failure

When fewer than half of the followers fail, the etcd cluster can still accept requests and make progress without any major disruption. For example, two follower failures will not affect a five member etcd cluster’s operation. However, clients will lose connectivity to the failed members. Client libraries should hide these interruptions from users for read requests by automatically reconnecting to other members. Operators should expect the system load on the other members to increase due to the reconnections.

## Leader failure

When a leader fails, the etcd cluster automatically elects a new leader. The election does not happen instantly once the leader fails. It takes about an election timeout to elect a new leader since the failure detection model is timeout based.

During the leader election the cluster cannot process any writes. Write requests sent during the election are queued for processing until a new leader is elected.

Writes already sent to the old leader but not yet committed may be lost. The new leader has the power to rewrite any uncommitted entries from the previous leader. From the user perspective, some write requests might time out after a new leader election. However, no committed writes are ever lost.

The new leader extends timeouts automatically for all leases. This mechanism ensures a lease will not expire before the granted TTL even if it was granted by the old leader.

## Majority failure

When the majority members of the cluster fail, the etcd cluster fails and cannot accept more writes.

The etcd cluster can only recover from a majority failure once the majority of members become available. If a majority of members cannot come back online, then the operator must start [disaster recovery][unrecoverable] to recover the cluster.

Once a majority of members works, the etcd cluster elects a new leader automatically and returns to a healthy state. The new leader extends timeouts automatically for all leases. This mechanism ensures no lease expires due to server side unavailability.

## Network partition

A network partition is similar to a minor followers failure or a leader failure. A network partition divides the etcd cluster into two parts; one with a member majority and the other with a member minority. The majority side becomes the available cluster and the minority side is unavailable. There is no “split-brain” in etcd because cluster members are explicitly added/removed with each such change is approved by the current majority of members.

If the leader is on the majority side, then from the majority point of view the failure is a minority follower failure. If the leader is on the minority side, then it is a leader failure. The leader on the minority side steps down and the majority side elects a new leader.

Once the network partition clears, the minority side automatically recognizes the leader from the majority side and recovers its state.

## Failure during bootstrapping

A cluster bootstrap is only successful if all required members successfully start. If any failure happens during bootstrapping, remove the data directories on all members and re-bootstrap the cluster with a new cluster-token or new discovery token.

Of course, it is possible to recover a failed bootstrapped cluster like recovering a running cluster. However, it almost always takes more time and resources to recover that cluster than bootstrapping a new one, since there is no data to recover.

For read requests, client libraries should hide these interruptions from users by automatically reconnecting to other members. Operators should expect the system load on the other members to increase because of those reconnections.

## Leader failure

When a leader fails, the etcd cluster automatically elects a new one. The election does not happen instantly. Because failure detection is timeout based, electing a new leader takes about an election timeout.

The cluster cannot process any writes during the leader election. Write requests sent during the election are queued and processed once a new leader is elected.

Writes already sent to the old leader but not yet committed may be lost, because the new leader has the power to rewrite any uncommitted entries from the previous leader. From the user's perspective, some write requests might time out after a new leader election. However, no committed writes are ever lost.

The new leader extends timeouts automatically for all leases. This ensures a lease will not expire before its granted TTL, even if the old leader granted it.

## Majority failure

When the majority of the cluster's members fail, the etcd cluster fails and cannot accept more writes.

The cluster can only recover from a majority failure once a majority of members become available again. If a majority of members cannot come back online, the operator must start [disaster recovery][unrecoverable] to recover the cluster.

Once a majority of members works, the etcd cluster elects a new leader automatically and returns to a healthy state. The new leader extends timeouts automatically for all leases. This ensures no lease expires because of server side unavailability.

## Network partition

A network partition resembles either a minor followers failure or a leader failure. A partition splits the etcd cluster into two parts: one with a member majority and one with a member minority. The majority side becomes the available cluster, and the minority side is unavailable. etcd has no "split-brain", because cluster members are explicitly added and removed, and each such change is approved by the current majority of members.

If the leader is on the majority side, the majority sees the event as a minority follower failure. If the leader is on the minority side, the event is a leader failure: the leader on the minority side steps down, and the majority side elects a new leader.

Once the network partition clears, the minority side automatically recognizes the leader from the majority side and recovers its state.

## Failure during bootstrapping

A cluster bootstrap succeeds only if all required members start successfully. If any failure happens during bootstrapping, remove the data directories on all members and re-bootstrap the cluster with a new cluster-token or a new discovery token.

Recovering a failed bootstrapped cluster is possible, just as with a running cluster. However, since there is no data to recover, it almost always costs more time and resources than simply bootstrapping a new one.

migration-etcd-3-5.title: Upgrade etcd from 3.4 to 3.5
migration-etcd-3-5.source:
### Server upgrade checklists

#### Upgrade requirements

To upgrade an existing etcd deployment to 3.5, the running cluster must be 3.4 or greater. If it's before 3.4, please [upgrade to 3.4](../upgrade_3_3/) before upgrading to 3.5.

Also, to ensure a smooth rolling upgrade, the running cluster must be healthy. Check the health of the cluster by using the `etcdctl endpoint health` command before proceeding.

#### Preparation

Before upgrading etcd, always test the services relying on etcd in a staging environment before deploying the upgrade to the production environment.

Before beginning, [download the snapshot backup](../../op-guide/maintenance/#snapshot-backup). Should something go wrong with the upgrade, it is possible to use this backup to [downgrade](#downgrade) back to existing etcd version. Please note that the `snapshot` command only backs up the v3 data. For v2 data, see [backing up v2 datastore](/docs/v2.3/admin_guide#backing-up-the-datastore).

#### Mixed versions

While upgrading, an etcd cluster supports mixed versions of etcd members, and operates with the protocol of the lowest common version. The cluster is only considered upgraded once all of its members are upgraded to version 3.5. Internally, etcd members negotiate with each other to determine the overall cluster version, which controls the reported version and the supported features.

#### Limitations

Note: If the cluster only has v3 data and no v2 data, it is not subject to this limitation.

If the cluster is serving a v2 data set larger than 50MB, each newly upgraded member may take up to two minutes to catch up with the existing cluster. Check the size of a recent snapshot to estimate the total data size. In other words, it is safest to wait for 2 minutes between upgrading each member.

For a much larger total data size, 100MB or more , this one-time process might take even more time. Administrators of very large etcd clusters of this magnitude can feel free to contact the [etcd team][etcd-contact] before upgrading, and we'll be happy to provide advice on the procedure.

#### Downgrade

If all members have been upgraded to v3.5, the cluster will be upgraded to v3.5, and downgrade from this completed state is **not possible**. If any single member is still v3.4, however, the cluster and its operations remains "v3.4", and it is possible from this mixed cluster state to return to using a v3.4 etcd binary on all members.

Please [download the snapshot backup](../../op-guide/maintenance/#snapshot-backup) to make downgrading the cluster possible even after it has been completely upgraded.

### Server upgrade checklists

#### Upgrade requirements

To upgrade an etcd deployment to 3.5, the running cluster must be 3.4 or later. If it is older than 3.4, [upgrade to 3.4](../upgrade_3_3/) first.

#### Preparation

Always test the services that depend on etcd in a staging environment. Do this before you deploy the upgrade to the production environment.

Before you start, [download the snapshot backup](../../op-guide/maintenance/#snapshot-backup). If the upgrade goes wrong, you can use this backup to [downgrade](#downgrade) to the existing etcd version. The `snapshot` command backs up only the v3 data. For v2 data, see [backing up v2 datastore](/docs/v2.3/admin_guide#backing-up-the-datastore).

#### Mixed versions

During an upgrade, an etcd cluster supports members that run different versions. The cluster operates with the protocol of the lowest common version. The cluster counts as upgraded only after every member runs version 3.5. The members negotiate with each other to determine the cluster version. That version controls the reported version and the supported features.

#### Limitations

This limitation does not apply to a cluster that holds only v3 data and no v2 data.

If the cluster serves a v2 data set larger than 50MB, each upgraded member can take up to two minutes to catch up with the cluster. Check the size of a recent snapshot to estimate the total data size. It is safest to wait two minutes between the upgrade of each member.

For a total data size of 100MB or more, this one-time process can take longer. If you administer a cluster of this size, you may contact the [etcd team][etcd-contact] before you upgrade. The team will advise you on the procedure.

After all members run v3.5, the cluster is upgraded to v3.5. From this state, a downgrade is **not possible**. If one member still runs v3.4, the cluster and its operations remain "v3.4". From this mixed state, you can return every member to a v3.4 etcd binary.

[Download the snapshot backup](../../op-guide/maintenance/#snapshot-backup) to make a downgrade possible even after the cluster is fully upgraded.

---
title: "Gopls: Troubleshooting"
---

If you suspect that `gopls` is crashing or not working correctly, please follow the troubleshooting steps below.

If `gopls` is using too much memory, please follow the steps under [Memory usage](#debug-memory-usage).

## Steps

VS Code users should follow [their troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/golang/vscode-go/blob/master/docs/troubleshooting.md), which has more a more specific version of these instructions.

1. Verify that your project is in good shape by working with it outside of your editor. Running a command like `go build ./...` in the workspace directory will compile everything. For modules, `go mod tidy` is another good check, though it may modify your `go.mod`.
1. Check that your editor isn't showing any diagnostics that indicate a problem with your workspace. They may appear as diagnostics on a Go file's package declaration, diagnostics in a go.mod file, or as a status or progress message. Problems in the workspace configuration can cause many different symptoms. See the [workspace setup instructions](workspace.md) for help.
1. Make sure `gopls` is up to date by following the [installation instructions](index.md#installation), then [restarting gopls](#restart-gopls).
1. Optionally, [ask for help](#ask-for-help) on Gophers Slack.
1. Finally, [report the issue](#file-an-issue) to the `gopls` developers.

## Restart `gopls`

`gopls` has no persistent state, so restarting it will fix transient problems. This is good and bad: good, because you can keep working, and bad, because you won't be able to debug the issue until it recurs.

In most cases, closing all your open editors will guarantee that `gopls` is killed and restarted. If you don't want to do that, there may be an editor command you can use to restart only `gopls`. Note that some `vim` configurations keep the server alive for a while after the editor exits; you may need to explicitly kill `gopls` if you use `vim`.

## Ask for help

Gophers Slack has active editor-specific channels like [#emacs](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C0HKHULEM), [#vim](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C07GBR52P), and [#vscode](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C2B4L99RS) that can help debug further. If you're confident the problem is with `gopls`, you can go straight to [#gopls](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/CJZH85XCZ). Invites are [available to everyone](https://invite.slack.golangbridge.org). Come prepared with a short description of the issue, and try to be available to answer questions for a while afterward.

## File an issue

We can't diagnose a problem from just a description. When filing an issue, please include as much as possible of the following information:

1. Your editor and any settings you have configured (for example, your VSCode `settings.json` file).
1. A sample program that reproduces the issue, if possible.
1. The output of `gopls version` on the command line.
1. A complete gopls log file from a session where the issue occurred. It should have a `go env for <workspace folder>` log line near the beginning. It's also helpful to tell us the timestamp the problem occurred, so we can find it the log. See the [instructions](#capture-logs) for information on how to capture gopls logs.

Your editor may have a command that fills out some of the necessary information, such as `:GoReportGitHubIssue` in `vim-go`. Otherwise, use the [Go issue tracker](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/new?title=x%2Ftools%2Fgopls%3A%20%3Cfill%20this%20in%3E).

## Capture logs

You may have to change your editor's configuration to pass a `-logfile` flag to gopls.

To increase the level of detail in your logs, start `gopls` with the `-rpc.trace` flag. To start a debug server that will allow you to see profiles and memory usage, start `gopls` with `serve --debug=localhost:6060`. You will then be able to view debug information by navigating to `localhost:6060`.

If you are unsure of how to pass a flag to `gopls` through your editor, please see the [documentation for your editor](index.md#editors).

## Debug memory usage

`gopls` automatically writes out memory debug information when your usage exceeds 1GB. This information can be found in your temporary directory with names like `gopls.1234-5GiB-withnames.zip`. On Windows, your temporary directory will be located at `%TMP%`, and on Unixes, it will be `$TMPDIR`, which is usually `/tmp`. Please [file an issue](#file-an-issue) with this memory debug information attached. If you are uncomfortable sharing the package names of your code, you can share the `-nonames` zip instead, but it's much less useful.

If you think `gopls` is crashing or misbehaving, work through the steps below.

If `gopls` is using too much memory, jump to [Memory usage](#debug-memory-usage).

## Steps

VS Code users should follow [their troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/golang/vscode-go/blob/master/docs/troubleshooting.md), which gives a more specific version of these instructions.

1. Check that your project is healthy outside your editor. Run `go build ./...` in the workspace directory to compile everything. For modules, `go mod tidy` is another good check, but note it may modify your `go.mod`.
1. Look for editor diagnostics that point to a workspace problem. They can show up on a Go file's package declaration, in a go.mod file, or as a status or progress message. A misconfigured workspace causes many different symptoms. See the [workspace setup instructions](workspace.md) for help.
1. Update `gopls` using the [installation instructions](index.md#installation), then [restart gopls](#restart-gopls).
1. Optionally, [ask for help](#ask-for-help) on Gophers Slack.
1. If nothing works, [report the issue](#file-an-issue) to the `gopls` developers.

## Restart `gopls`

`gopls` keeps no persistent state, so a restart clears up transient problems. That cuts both ways: you can get back to work, but you can't debug the issue until it happens again.

Closing all open editors will kill and restart `gopls` in most cases. If you'd rather not do that, your editor may have a command to restart only `gopls`. Note that some `vim` configurations keep the server alive for a while after the editor exits, so with `vim` you may need to kill `gopls` explicitly.

## Ask for help

Gophers Slack has active editor-specific channels — [#emacs](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C0HKHULEM), [#vim](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C07GBR52P), and [#vscode](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C2B4L99RS) — that can help you debug further. If you're sure the problem is with `gopls`, go straight to [#gopls](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/CJZH85XCZ). Invites are [available to everyone](https://invite.slack.golangbridge.org). Bring a short description of the issue, and try to stay available to answer questions afterward.

## File an issue

A description alone isn't enough for us to diagnose a problem. When filing an issue, include as much of the following as you can:

1. Your editor and any settings you've configured (for example, your VSCode `settings.json` file).
1. A sample program that reproduces the issue, if possible.
1. The output of `gopls version` on the command line.
1. A complete gopls log file from a session where the issue happened. It should have a `go env for <workspace folder>` log line near the beginning. Telling us the timestamp of the problem also helps, so we can find it in the log. See the [instructions](#capture-logs) for how to capture gopls logs.

Your editor may have a command that fills in some of this information, such as `:GoReportGitHubIssue` in `vim-go`. Otherwise, use the [Go issue tracker](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/new?title=x%2Ftools%2Fgopls%3A%20%3Cfill%20this%20in%3E).

You may need to change your editor's configuration to pass a `-logfile` flag to gopls.

For more detailed logs, start `gopls` with the `-rpc.trace` flag. To start a debug server showing profiles and memory usage, start `gopls` with `serve --debug=localhost:6060`, then view the debug information at `localhost:6060`.

If you're not sure how to pass a flag to `gopls` from your editor, see the [documentation for your editor](index.md#editors).

When usage goes over 1GB, `gopls` writes out memory debug information automatically. Look in your temporary directory for files named like `gopls.1234-5GiB-withnames.zip`. On Windows the temporary directory is `%TMP%`; on Unixes it's `$TMPDIR`, usually `/tmp`. Please [file an issue](#file-an-issue) and attach this memory debug information. If you'd rather not share your code's package names, you can send the `-nonames` zip instead, though it's much less useful.

This repo defines **PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English)** — a controlled-English writing standard for software communication, plus a Claude Code skill and linter that enforce it.

**The problem it's solving:** AI coding agents (and human engineers) tend to write bloated, hedge-y prose — passive voice, synonym rotation ("verify/validate/confirm/check" for the same action), stacked qualifiers, marketing fluff ("robust", "seamless"), buried warnings before destructive commands. That style is slow to parse, especially for a reader who's tired, in a hurry, or not a native English speaker skimming a pasted Slack excerpt. PSTE is a restricted vocabulary and grammar — one word per meaning, simple tenses only, short sentences, active voice, named actors, results stated first — aimed specifically at things like READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, runbooks, incident reports, and agent chat output. It's explicitly modeled after ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English, used in aerospace maintenance manuals), but reimplemented from scratch for software vocabulary (`refactor`, `deploy`, `merge`, `rollback`) rather than copying ASD's aerospace dictionary, which is trademarked and restricted.

**Who it's for:** teams and individuals who want an agent (or their own team's docs) to produce consistently plain, unambiguous technical prose — think release notes, runbooks, error messages, and any output that gets pasted around and read out of context. It ships as three things: a spec (`spec/PSTE-1.md`, written RFC-style with MUST/SHOULD/MAY), a Claude Code skill (`skill/SKILL.md`) that gets an agent to write in this style continuously across a session, and a standalone linter (`lib/pste_lint.py`) with zero dependencies that can run as a pre-commit hook to check conformance.

**What it deliberately does not claim**, and this is the part the repo is unusually insistent about: it does not make output more correct, more thoughtful, or smarter — only more readable in *form*. A document can pass every PSTE check and still be wrong or empty; the spec calls that a defect, not an edge case. It also doesn't claim its own effectiveness is proven yet: the only human-comprehension evidence it can point to is a 1996 aviation-industry study on human-authored maintenance manuals, not software text or AI-generated text. Its own evaluation tooling (`evals/`) — readability scoring and a fact-loss checker — has been built but never run against real readers, and the repo is explicit that until a real comprehension trial happens, the honest claim is "passes automated checks," not "is easier to read." It's also careful to say its own linter output shouldn't be read as a quality score, because a rewrite can pass by simply dropping information, which the checker can't see but a separate faithfulness check tries to catch.

AI coding agents and human engineers write bloated, hedged prose. The common faults are the passive voice, rotated synonyms ("verify", "validate", "confirm", and "check" for one action), stacked qualifiers, marketing words ("robust", "seamless"), and warnings buried after a destructive command.

It targets README files, pull request descriptions, commit messages, runbooks, incident reports, and the chat output of an agent.

The standard follows the model of ASD-STE100, which is Simplified Technical English, used in maintenance manuals for aerospace. The authors wrote PSTE from scratch for software vocabulary such as `refactor`, `deploy`, `merge`, and `rollback`.   Read the repository at /repo and explain how the skill makes sure it is still applied late in a long session, after the conversation has been compacted. Describe the mechanisms and why each one exists. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

The mechanism is a plugin with two hooks plus a file on disk, not anything in the conversation itself — that's the whole point, since conversation content is exactly what compaction throws away.

**1. State lives in a file, not in the transcript.** `pste-config.js` stores the active level (`off`/`lite`/`pste`/`strict`) in `~/.claude/.pste-active`, written atomically (temp file + rename) and with a symlink check so nothing can hijack the write. Compaction summarizes or drops old messages, but it can't touch the filesystem, so the moment a user runs `/pste strict` or says "use pste," that choice survives indefinitely — a fresh session or a post-compaction turn reads the same flag file and picks up exactly where it left off, rather than resetting to some default.

**2. A `SessionStart` hook re-injects the full rulebook.** `pste-activate.js` runs on every `SessionStart` event. In Claude Code, compaction actually fires `SessionStart` again (with a different "source"), so this hook doesn't just run once at the beginning of a conversation — it runs again right after compaction happens. It reads `SKILL.md` fresh off disk each time (never a cached copy, so it can't drift out of sync with the documented rules) and dumps the full rule set with examples back into context. The comment in that file makes the reasoning explicit: a two-sentence style reminder fades from a model's attention after a few turns, and compaction erases it outright, so the fix is to reload the complete instructions at exactly the moment compaction would otherwise have wiped them out.

**3. A `UserPromptSubmit` hook adds a reminder on every single turn.** `pste-tracker.js` runs before each user message is processed and injects a short, level-specific reminder ("PSTE ACTIVE (strict). Result first. Active voice...") into context. This is deliberately not the full rule set — repeating everything every turn would cost more than it's worth — but it's a constant low-cost nudge that keeps the instruction present in the model's near-term attention between the (comparatively rare) full reloads from `SessionStart`. This is what stops "drift back to loose prose after many turns," which is the exact failure mode called out in `SKILL.md`'s own "Persistence" section.

Together these three layers cover the two ways long sessions lose instructions: the file solves the problem of losing *which setting was chosen*, the `SessionStart` reload solves the problem of losing the *full rule text* right when compaction happens, and the per-turn reminder solves the slower problem of the model's attention drifting away from an instruction it received many turns ago.

synth-evidence.source:
---

question: |
  Read the repository at /repo and explain what evidence supports the claim that its controlled English helps a reader. Cover what has been measured, what has not, and which measures the project rejected. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

I read through the project (it's a controlled-English writing standard called PSTE, modeled loosely on ASD-STE100) and traced every place it makes or examines the "helps a reader" claim. Here's the honest picture, which is actually laid out with unusual candor in the repo itself.

## What's actually been measured

**One real study backs the core claim, and it's not about this project.** Chervak, Drury and Ouellette (1996) tested 175 aircraft technicians reading Simplified English aircraft workcards. Comprehension went from 76% to 86% overall, and from 69% to 87% for non-native English readers. That's a genuine human-subjects result, and it's the reason the project exists — but it's scoped to aerospace maintenance text, written by humans, read by humans. Nothing about software documentation, nothing about machine-generated text.

**One weak pilot touches the actual use case (AI-generated controlled English).** A blog post experiment (woosal1337, linked in README.md and SOURCES.md) found a style rubric cut "AI slop" markers by half or more. The project's own writeup is unusually blunt about the problems: six prompts, one run each, a metric that counts the same markers the prompt tells the model to avoid, and on one of two models tested, a simpler rubric did just as well or better. The repo calls this "a pilot, not proof" — twice, in two different files.

**Two homegrown proxy measures exist and run offline**, in `evals/`:
- `readability.py` scores vocabulary coverage against thresholds from Nation (2006) and Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010) — real research tying vocabulary coverage to comprehension scores, with 95%/98% coverage thresholds for supported vs. independent reading.
- `faithfulness.py` checks whether a rewrite dropped or altered numbers, units, identifiers, negations, or obligations — guarding against the specific failure mode where a rewrite reads more smoothly but quietly loses a fact.

Both are explicitly labeled as proxies, not comprehension tests.
